extracted.intended_audience: USPTO examiners and patent practitioners handling U.S. design patent prosecution
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and examiner form paragraphs for handling restriction, grouping of embodiments, double patenting rejections, priority claims, and related procedural requirements in U.S. design patent prosecution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design protection and segregable parts
rubrics_metrics.description: Design protection does not extend to patentably distinct segregable parts of a design; a design patent covers only the design disclosed as an entirety.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If parts are patentably distinct segregable parts, the only way to protect them is separate patents (Ex parte Sanford; Blumcraft v. Ladd). Combination/subcombination subject matter, if patentably distinct, must be supported by separate claims; only a single claim is permissible in a design patent application (In re Rubinfield).

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentably distinct vs patentably indistinct embodiments
rubrics_metrics.description: Embodiments that are patentably indistinct may be included together as a single inventive concept; embodiments that are patentably distinct do not constitute a single inventive concept and thus may not be included in the same design application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners group embodiments considered obvious variations of one another as patentably indistinct (In re Rubinfield). If embodiments are patentably distinct, they should be separated into distinct groups and restriction may be required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grouping of embodiments by appearance and scope
rubrics_metrics.description: When an application discloses multiple embodiments, the examiner may divide them into patentably distinct groups of designs (e.g., Group I, Group II) based on differences in appearance or scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Form paragraphs provide placeholders to list embodiments and groups and instruct examiners/applicants to add embodiments as necessary and to insert explanations of differences between designs (examples: Figs.1–5 directed to cup & saucer; Figs.6–9 directed to saucer).

rubrics_metrics.name: Restriction requirement under 35 U.S.C. 121
rubrics_metrics.description: Restriction is required under 35 U.S.C. 121 to one of the patentably distinct groups of designs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A reply to this requirement must include an election of a single group for prosecution on the merits even if the requirement is traversed (37 CFR 1.143). Any reply not including an election will be held nonresponsive. Applicant is requested to cancel all drawing figures and corresponding descriptions directed to nonelected groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Traversing a restriction – burden of proof
rubrics_metrics.description: If applicant traverses the restriction on the grounds that groups are not patentably distinct, applicant must present evidence now of record showing the groups to be obvious variations of one another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If groups remain and are determined not to be patentably distinct, any rejection of one group over prior art will apply equally to all other groups; no argument asserting patentability based on differences between groups will be considered once groups are determined to comprise a single inventive concept.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common embodiment included in multiple groups – qualifying statement
rubrics_metrics.description: A common embodiment may be included in more than a single group if it is patentably indistinct from other embodiments, to give applicant broad choices in election.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the common embodiment is elected, applicant is advised that it should not be included in any continuing application to avoid a double patenting rejection under 35 U.S.C. 171 in the new application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cancellation/withdrawal of nonelected groups (post-election procedures)
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedures for withdrawing, canceling, or treating nonelected groups after election or traverse (including final requirements).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Group withdrawn from consideration by examiner under 37 CFR 1.142(b) when nonelected. If restriction requirement is final, applicant must cancel nonelected groups or take other timely action (37 CFR 1.144). If application otherwise in condition for allowance except for nonelected groups, such groups may be canceled without right to petition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Double patenting rejection types
rubrics_metrics.description: There are generally two types of double patenting rejections: (1) the 'same invention' type based on 35 U.S.C. 171 and (2) the nonstatutory (judicially created) double patenting rejections grounded in public policy (including obviousness-type and differing scope).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nonstatutory double patenting is primarily intended to prevent unjustified timewise extension of the patent term. The charts in MPEP § 804 outline procedures for handling double patenting rejections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Same-invention double patenting (35 U.S.C. 171) criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: A statutory design-design double patenting rejection under 35 U.S.C. 171 prevents issuance of a second patent for a design already patented; requires identical designs with identical scope to be twice claimed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For this type of rejection to be proper, identical designs with identical scope must be twice claimed (In re Goodman). A terminal disclaimer may not be used to overcome a 'same invention' type double patenting rejection (In re Thorington; In re Swett). Use form paragraph 15.23.02 following such rejections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design-utility and design-design 'same invention' considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: A design-utility 'same invention' double patenting rejection is based on judicial doctrine since certain statutory sections cannot be applied against both claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 'same invention' type, whether statutory or nonstatutory, cannot be overcome by terminal disclaimer. Use the designated form paragraph sequence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonstatutory double patenting — obviousness-type criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: An obviousness-type nonstatutory double patenting rejection applies to claims directed to the same inventive concept with different appearances which are obvious variations of each other; differences are not patentably distinct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The obviousness standard of 35 U.S.C. 103(a) applies: differences must be de minimis/unrelated to overall aesthetic or obvious to a designer of ordinary skill in the art in view of prior art or case law. This type of rejection may be overcome by submission of a terminal disclaimer if conditions are met (common ownership).

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonstatutory double patenting — differing scope criteria (A/B/C test)
rubrics_metrics.description: A nonstatutory differing-scope double patenting rejection is appropriate if: (A) the difference in scope is de minimis and unrelated to overall aesthetic appearance; (B) patent protection for the design, fully disclosed in and covered by the claim of the reference, would be extended by allowance of the later claim; and (C) no terminal disclaimer has been filed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This situation often involves a combination (narrow claim) vs a subcombination/element (broad claim). Examiner must determine whether the narrower claim is fully disclosed in and covered by the broader claim reference (including title, description, or broken-line drawings). If not fully disclosed, the double patenting rejection is inappropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provisional double patenting handling and disposition
rubrics_metrics.description: How to handle provisional double patenting rejections when conflicting claims have not yet issued as patents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a provisional double patenting rejection is the only remaining rejection in two conflicting applications, withdraw that rejection in one (e.g., earlier filing date) and permit it to issue; maintain the provisional rejection in the other application to be converted when the first issues. When more than two conflicting applications exist and one is allowed, cross-reject remaining applications. For these rejections to be appropriate, there must be at least one inventor in common or common assignee.

rubrics_metrics.name: One-way vs two-way obviousness determinations
rubrics_metrics.description: Determination whether to make a one-way or two-way obviousness determination when issuing nonstatutory double patenting rejections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criteria for one-way vs two-way are set forth in MPEP § 804. In design-utility situations, the majority opinion in Carman Inds. v. Wahl (and In re Dembiczak) suggests a two-way obviousness determination may be necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terminal disclaimer use for nonstatutory double patenting
rubrics_metrics.description: A timely filed terminal disclaimer in compliance with 37 CFR 1.321(c) may be used to overcome an actual or provisional nonstatutory double patenting rejection provided the conflicting application or patent is commonly owned with this application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Terminal disclaimer is intended to remove potential harm to the public by issuing a second patent, not to remove a patent as prior art (see MPEP § 804). Effective Jan 1, 1994, a registered attorney/agent of record may sign; a terminal disclaimer signed by an assignee must comply with 37 CFR 3.73(b). Form paragraph 15.24.06 must precede nonstatutory double patenting rejections (except 'same invention' type).

rubrics_metrics.name: Form paragraph procedures for obviousness-type double patenting (single reference)
rubrics_metrics.description: Standard form paragraph language to reject a claim under the obviousness-type double patenting doctrine based on a single prior patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Insert conflicting prior U.S. patent number and an explanation why claims are not patentably distinct. Precede with paragraph 15.24.06 and follow with form paragraph 15.67 (rationale for 103(a) rejection).

rubrics_metrics.name: Form paragraph procedures for obviousness-type double patenting (multiple references)
rubrics_metrics.description: Standard form paragraph language to reject a claim under the obviousness-type double patenting doctrine based on multiple references.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Insert conflicting patent number and secondary reference(s), and explain basis for rejection including how a designer of ordinary skill would have been led to combine references. Precede with paragraph 15.24.06 and follow with form paragraph 15.68 (rationale for 103(a) with multiple references).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationale for 35 U.S.C. 103(a) rejections — overall appearance test
rubrics_metrics.description: Unobviousness in design patents is determined by the overall appearance of the claimed design compared with the prior art, not by minute details or small variations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite In re Frick and In re Lamb. Examiner should articulate why overall appearance is unobvious when making a 103(a) rejection; use form paragraphs 15.67 (single reference) and 15.68 (multiple references) as applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: 35 U.S.C. 102(e) provisional rejection for common inventor/assignee
rubrics_metrics.description: The claim may be provisionally rejected under 35 U.S.C. 102(e) as being anticipated by a copending application or patent which has a common inventor or assignee and an earlier effective U.S. filing date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provisional rejection is based on presumption of future patenting of the conflicting copending application. It may be overcome by showing derivation under 37 CFR 1.132 (that the disclosure was derived from the inventor of this application) or by showing an earlier date of invention under 37 CFR 1.131. Use appropriate form paragraphs and insert 'inventor' or 'assignee' in bracketed fields as needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identical claim with common assignee — priority resolution requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: When a claim is directed to the same invention as a claim of a commonly assigned copending application, the issue of priority under 35 U.S.C. 102(f)/(g) must be resolved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Since PTO normally will not institute interferences between commonly owned applications, the assignee is required to state which entity is the prior inventor of the conflicting subject matter. A terminal disclaimer has no effect here because the basis is priority of invention; failure to comply will result in abandonment of the application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonstatutory double patenting based solely on improper timewise extension
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim may be rejected under the nonstatutory double patenting doctrine if allowance of the later claim would improperly extend the right to exclude granted in an earlier patent (differing scope based solely on timewise extension).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use when subject matter of the later claim is fully disclosed in issued patent commonly owned or with common inventorship and the claims are not patentably distinct (Blumcraft v. Ladd; In re Schneller). Precede with form paragraph 15.24.06.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provisional nonstatutory double patenting with another application (differing scope)
rubrics_metrics.description: A provisional rejection may be made under the nonstatutory differing-scope doctrine over a copending application if allowance of the claim would improperly extend the right to exclude granted in any patent that may issue on the copending application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use only when the subject matter of the claim is fully disclosed in the copending application which is commonly owned or has common inventorship and the claims are not patentably distinct. Precede with form paragraph 15.24.06.

rubrics_metrics.name: Priority under 35 U.S.C. 119(a)-(d) — six-month rule for designs
rubrics_metrics.description: To obtain the benefit of an earlier foreign filing date for a design, the U.S. application must be filed within six months of the earliest foreign application filing date; the period for designs is six months (35 U.S.C. 172).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 35 U.S.C.119(e) does not apply to designs. Design applications may not claim priority to a provisional application under 37 CFR 1.78(a)(3). If priority papers are filed late (more than six months), the claim for priority cannot be based on that application and papers are returned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural requirements for claiming foreign priority under treaties
rubrics_metrics.description: When claiming priority based on treaty filings (e.g., Hague Agreement, Benelux), certain information must be supplied: the treaty name, at least one other country where the application has effect, and the national or intergovernmental authority that received the application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In addition to application number and date, provide the treaty name, a country (other than the U.S.) where the application has effect, and the name/location of the receiving authority. The PTO may require certified copies and translations; see MPEP Chapter 200 and 37 CFR 1.55 for details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right of priority under 35 U.S.C. 119(b) — certification and timing
rubrics_metrics.description: No design application is entitled to right of priority under 35 U.S.C. 119(b) unless a claim and a certified copy of the original foreign application, specification and drawings are filed in the USPTO before the issue fee is paid or at such time during pendency as required by the Commissioner (not earlier than six months).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Certification shall be made by the foreign Patent Office or other proper authority and show the date of the application and filing of specification and papers. Commissioner may require translation and other information. The notation requirement on application file wrappers when foreign priority is claimed is in MPEP § 202.03.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examination of priority papers for design patents
rubrics_metrics.description: Unlike some practice, in design patent applications the priority papers will normally be inspected to determine that the foreign application is for the same invention as the U.S. application (35 U.S.C. 119).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If inspection indicates the prior foreign application was not for the same invention as claimed, the priority claim is improper and the papers are returned. Attention is directed to handling cases where an actual model was originally filed in Germany (MPEP § 201.14(b)).
